newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end higher, Fed rate hike questioned.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end higher, Fed rate hike questioned.

text.p: Treasury prices closed higher Thursday, boosted by tame inflation news and speculation the Federal Reserve will move by only 25 basis points, if at all, at its upcoming September 24 policy meeting.

The Producer Price Index for August rose 0.3 percent. But the market was encouraged by a slip in the so-called core rate, which excludes the volatile food and energy components. It fell 0.1 percent and prompted traders to buy the intermediate and long term issues of the yield curve.

Some analysts said the bond market has priced in a 25-basis point interest rate hike by the Fed for September 24, but that traders are now beginning to consider the possibility the Fed may not raise rates at that meeting.
"The yield curve is not really pricing in a certainty, but a likelihood of 25 (basis points)" said Joseph Liro, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy. "But not even that is universally accepted."
The benchmark 6.75 percent 30-year Treasury bond closed up 14/32 at 93-31/32 to yield 7.08 percent. The 6.125 percent two-year note ended up 3/32 at 99-23/32 to yield 6.28 percent.

The Atlanta Fed Survey of business activity for August came in at 4.0 percent versus a revised a minus 1.2 percent, providing further evidence for the bond market that the economy is still chugging along at an above trend pace.

"Once again we're talking about an economic picture of steady growth and low inflation," said James Kenney, head of government securities trading at Prudential Securities. "The market has a difficult time with that. It's looking for the problem, the fly in the ointment, and the fact is we don't have one at the moment."

Just after midday, the market pulled back slightly off its highs when Reuters quoted a Fed source as saying some policymakers "would say it's time to take the insurance back, because it was an exploratory move, an insurance against weakness." The source was referring to the 25-basis point cut the Fed made in January.
"I think it was the Fed source comments on Reuters that took the market off its highs," said Kim Rupert, senior economist at MMS International. "At least it put a lid on things."
Some analysts said those comments are in line with the barrage of messages from Fed officials this week regarding the economy and inflation.
"The market is cautious, but also there is some degree of being impressed by how well it continues to hold in through all of these comments," said John Ryding, senior economist with Bear Stearns.
The long end later revisited its daily highs late in the trading session on short covering ahead of Friday's Consumer Price Index (CPI) and retail sales data for August.
"People are unwilling to run a long way with any information today given they are looking down the twin barrels of retail sales and CPI," Ryding said.

The consensus forecast calls for a 0.2 percent rise in both the overall and core rates of August CPI. Retail sales figures for August are expected to rise 0.7 percent overall and 0.4 percent excluding autos.

Three-month bill rates fell three basis points to 5.13 percent, six-month bill rates ended off three basis points at 5.26 percent, and one-year bill rates shed five basis points to close at 5.53 percent.
The Treasury's 6-1/2 percent five year note ended up 7/32 at 99-13/32 to yield 6.64 percent and its 7-percent 10-year note rose 11/32 to 100-28/32 to close with a yield of 6.87 percent.
